WARRINGTON CORPORATION GAS BILL. Purchase by and transfer to the Cor- poration of the undertaking, property, powers, and privileges, of the Warrington .Gas Light and Coke COmpsny. Power to maintain and enlarge Gas Works, and supply Gas, Borrowing of Money, Rates, and Assessments ; powers to contract with Local Authorities, Amendment and Incorporation of Acts, and other purposes.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that application is intended to be made to Parliament in the ensuing Session, by the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington, in the respective counties of Lancaster and Chester, (hereinafter called the Cor- poration), for an Ad for all or some of the following purposes, that is to say.

To confer on the Corporation powers to purchase and hold and to enable the Warrington Gas Light and Coke Company (hereinafter called the Company), to sell and transfer to the Corporation the undertaking lands, buildings, works, mains,. pipes, approaches, easements, powers, rights, and privileges of or belong- ing to, or possessed or enjoyed by the Company, and for that purpose to cot firm or give effect, subject to the approval of Parliament, to the provisions of an agreement dated the Twentieth day of October, 1876, and made between the Company of the one part, and the Corporation of the other part. To provide for the dissolution and winding up of the Company, and the distribution of the purchase money or annuitierr, and the assets of the Company among the several persons entitled thereto. And tha intended Acewill confer upon the Corpora- tion the following or aome of the following powers, namely :
To supply Gas for public and private purposes and otherwise carry on the undertaking of the Com- pany throughout the limits of supply of the Com- pany. -

- - To maintain, re-build, enlarge and repair on the lands specified in the schedule to the Warrington Gas Act, 1871, and which are situate in the borough of Warrington, in the county of Lancaster, and bounded on the North-East by Academy-street, on the North- West by Chrimes'-yard,.and a bouae and yard late in the occupation of Mr. Fanolough, but now of the Con- servative Club, on the South-West by Lower Bank- street and Upper Bank-street, and on the South-East by Mersey-street, and contain in the whole four acres little more or less, gas works, gasometers, retorts, ma- chinery, apparatus, buildings, approaches, works, and conveniences, and to manufacture and store gas and the several matters producible from the residual pro- ducts arising or resulting from the manufacture of gas, and also from time to time to purchase by agree- ment, or take on lease, and hold such other lands and property as they may find necessary for the storage of gas, or other purposes of the intended Act.

To convert, manufacture, sell and dispose of coke coal tar, and other residual products arising from the manufacture of gas; and to manufacture, purchase, sail, and let meters, fittings, and other apparatus, and to make contracts, with any persons, companies, or corporations in relation thereto. To lay down and maintain gas, mains, pipes, cul" verts, tramways. and other works in, through, under, over, or across, and for such purposes to cross, break up, alter, divert, or stop up either temporarily or perma- nently roads, !treats, highway footpaths, and,other pub. lie Places) bridges, canals, railways, tramways, sewers, drains, streams, brooks, water courses, and pipes, and to remove and alter telegraph wires throughout the limits of supply of the Company.

To apply to the purposes of the intended Ad, or any of them, any funds or money belonging or coming to them, or which they are or may be empowered to raise by rates, or otherwise under any public general or other Acts for the time beingin force, and to borrow further money for such purposes on the credit of their gas undertaking, and of the rates, rents, and charges which they are now authorised to make and levy, or may by the intended Act be authorised to make and levy, and to charge upon the rates, rents, and charges, or any of them, the payments to be made for the pur- chase of the gas undertaking, andto make provision for consolidating the sinking fund in respect of the monies now owing by the Corporation, with that provided under the intended Act.

To make, levy, and recover rates, rents, assessments, and other charges for the supply of gas and the sale and hire of meters and fittings, end other the purposes of the intended Act, and to increase, alter, repeal, or extinguish existing rates, rents, assessments, and charges, and to make new or increased rates, rents, assessments, and charges in lieu thereof, and to grant exemptions from rates, rents, assessments, and charges, and to compound with the owners and occupiers of houses and premises for the payment of such rates, rents, assessments and charges.

To enter into and carry into effect contracts and arrangements for the supply of gas with any Urban or other Sanitary or Local Authority, or the Trustees of any turnpike or other road, or any Highway Board, or any Surveyors of any highway, or Company, bodies, or persons within or outside the limits of supply of the Company; and the intended Act will confer all neces- sary powers in that behalf upon all such authorities, companies, trustees, bodies, and persons, and will en- able them to apply for the purposes of any such con- tract or arrangements any funds or moneys belonging to them, respectively, or under their control, and to raise money by rates or borrowing. To provide for the payment by the Corporation of all costs, charges, and expenses of and incident to OA preparing for obtaining and passing the intended Act or otherwise in relation thereto. The intended Act will incorporate with or without variation, and extend and apply to the purposes there- of, all or some of the powers and provisions of "The Gas Works Clauses Act, 1847," and "The Gas Works Clauses Act, 1871."

The intended Act will also incorporate and apply to the Corporation, or alter, amend, or repeal so: far as may be necessary the provisions of" The Warrington Gas 1847, "The Warrington Gas Act, 1871," TasheAc'karrington Improvement and Market Act, 18,5' 1 " and of the several Publio Health and Local Government Acts and Local Loans Act, and it will alter, vary, or extinguish all rights and privileges Fuleb would impede or interfere with any of the ob- jects aforesaid, and confer other powers, rights, and privileges. Print,* copies of the Bill for the intended Act will be deposited in the Private Bill Office of the House of 1876. Commons, on or before the 21st day of December,

PROTEST AGAINST AN EXORBITANT COUNTY RATE.

On Tuesday evening an adjourned meeting of rate- payers was held in the Assembly Room, Barlestown, Newton, to take into consideration the desirability of appealing against the exorbitant county rate assess- ment. The chair was occupied by lidr.W.Winstanley, the senior overseer.

The Cassassex said that about three months ago a deputation from the Financial Committee of the county were appointed to meet at Warrington to look into the assessment of the various townships con- nected with the Warrington Union, and that commit- tea found, when carrying out those duties, that the cottage property in Earlestown and Newton was too lightly assessed. He believed it arose in this way— about ten years ago the overeeers and others made a valuation of the township, and at that time there was a large nnmber ef cottages and a few shops unoccu- pied; in addition, the rates were very high, and it was thought right to take these circumstances into con- sideration, and reasonable allowances Were therefore made, in addition to the usual per centage of 15 or 20 per cent, deduction, in accordance with the rental of the property. This, of course, would naturally tend to pull down the assessment too low for the present , period; but although during the last few years they had gradually raised the assessment, it remained at too low s figure yet. All ratepayers must submit to a fair , and perfectly legal increase, established on a true basis. He believed that the ratepayers would have no objec- tion to pay whit was their honest proportion. (Hear, hear.) But when an attempt is made to saddle them with an increased assessment of £5,000, every rate- payer had a perfect right to object to it, and oppose it by all lawful means. (Applauqe.) They had gone carefully and honestly into this question from the rate books and other sources of information, and found that the present assessment was from £2,000 to £2,500 less than it ought to be. These figures were correct, and truly represented their fair, bounden responsibilities, but beyond £2,500 he was not willing to go. .(Hear, hear.) He was glad to see amongst them a spirit to act justly in this matter. The Financial Committee met at Warrington and theyassessed the whole of the townships belonging to their Union in one day, therefore he was not surprised that inequalities should occur, but if they could showiustifiable grounds on appealing against the excessive assessment of £5,000, which they could, undoubtedly, the matter would be set right. Their own assessment of from £2,000 to £2,500 meant an additional £175 a year to the ratepayers. He (the speaker) was sorry that he could not attend the meeting at Warrington,where he would have strongly ' opposed the exorbitant increase and would have given sound reasons for so doing. They had a remedy, however, which was plain and straight- forward, and that was to empower their overseers, along with Mr. Sutton, to attend in their behalf at Preston, on the appeal day, to get the matter righted. (Loud applause.)

Mr. B. Warms quite agreed with his collee,stue's views, for really if the assessment of £5 000 was ao- oopted it would be a great 'wrong, and necessitate an assessment on all property actually above its rental. Mr. H. HOUGHTON (assistant overseer) corroborated Mr. Winstanley's remarks, and added that after deal- ing equitably by putting everyone on a fair footing the township would be fully £2,500 short of the sum imposed upon it by the Financial Committee of the County, thu.s affording reasonable grounds for appeal. Mr. T. Foams remarked that in some districts of the Union, cottage and other property let at a much higher rent than at Earlestown and Newton, and it was quite likely that the Finance Committee had rated their dis- trict at the high rental by mistake. (Hear, hear.) After a general discussion on the question, in which Messrs. Dagnall, Williams, Howarth, Ball, and Corlett took part, Mr. RATCLLITZ proposed that the overseers, along with Mr. Sutton, be empowered to attend at Preston, with all necessary documents, on the day of appeal to take all right and proper steps for obtaining a fair ad- jus.nient of this important question. Mr. E. HOWARTH seconded the proposition which on being put to the meeting was heartily and unanimously Carried.
- A vote of thanks was awarded to Mr. W. E. Win- stanley for the able manner he had discharged the duties of Chairman, which was duly acknowledged, and the proceedings closed.

div.head: OUT-DOOR RELIEF. IMPORTANT PROPOSAL.
div.p: OUT-DOOR RELIEF. IMPORTANT PROPOSAL.

At the usual fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednesday last, At the request of the Chairman, Mr. HY. Braimmerose to lgive an account of a re- cent Poor-law conference held at Manchester, at which, amongst other subjects, the question of the Impropriety of giving out-door relief indiscriminately was discussed. The Chorlton-on-Medlock Union had adopted the following code of rules with great sue. 0555 :

I.—Out. door relief will for the future be allowed to persons of good charaler, who can satiety the guar- dians that their destitution has not been caused by im- providence or intemperance, and that whilst in work they did all they could to make provision against times of sickness or want of employment. .Those who cannot satisfy the guardians as to this will, if relieved at all, be required to enter the Workhouse with their

2.—Out-door relief will not be granted, except in special CM!, to any workmen or other operatives when on strike; to out-door labourers out of work through frost; or to any able-bodied person in good health who is only temporarily out of employment. Such persons will only be relieved inside the Work- house.

3.—Out-door relief will also be refused to persona of any of the following classes :—Single able-bodied men; single able-bodied women; abla-bodied women without children, or having only one child to support; married women (with or without families) left destitute through their libsbands having joined the militia, and being called up for training ; persons residing with relatives, where the united income of the family is sufficient for the support of all its members, whether such relatives are liable by law to support such appli- cant or not. Also, except in special cases, to—Married women (with or without families) whose husbands, having been convicted of crime, are undergoing a term of imprisonment; married women (with or with- out families) deserted by their husbands. The guar- dians give this warning in the hope that persons who have been in the habit of relying on assistance from the parish may endeavour, by thrift and economy, to make such provisions for themselves, instead of be- coming a burden upon the ratepayers, many of whom are not much better off than those who receive relief. The guardians also take this opportunity of intima- ting that they think it probable that, In the course of a very few years, out-door relief will be discontinued altogether, except in very urgent or special cases.

He found from inquiry that with out-door relief pau- perism extended, and with in•cloor relief it diminished. It was an unreasonable thing that the ratepayers should be called upon to contribute to the support of persons who had been left destitute by improvidence. He hoped some similar resolution to that adopted by the Chorlton-on-Medloek Union would be adopted by the Warrington Union, which would be highly bene- ficial to the ratepayers and ,also to the poor. (Hear, hear.) ,

Mr. BRAN expressed concurrence with Mr. Blackly's views on the matter, and hoped that similar rules to those read would be adopted. Mr. WINBTANLET said the fact of giving relief to women with large families created pauperism, and in the majority of instances the children of parents who had been relieved came back themselves to the Guar. dians as paupers.

The Manx also protested against the too ready ad- ministration of medical relief, and regarded as most wholesome the law which disfranchised voters because they had pauperised themselves with receiving medical relief. Mr. GARNETT crndemned the practice of giving re- lief to women whose husbands had been sent to prison, and said it was like setting a premium on crime.

Mr. PAhxymos said while agreeing in the main with what had fallen from the lips of the Guardians present he believed that there had been oases before the Board in which persons had been brought to poverty and destitution through no fault of their own, and who were really deserving of out-door relief. (Hear, hear.) At the same time he expressed his sorrow at seeing workingmen who had been earning good wages for a lengthened period, brought to pauperism because they had been out of work a fortnight. Such conduct on the part of workingmen deserved the most severe con- demnation, and ought not to be countenanced. (Hear, hear.)

After an interesting discussion, at the request of the Chairman, Mr. Bleekly consented to bring forward the subject for ?Tactical adoption within a month,. the Chorlton-on-medlock rules to be printed and eireu• lated, meanwhile, amongst the Guardians.

div.head: PULLMAN TRAIN WRECKED.
div.p: A PULLMAN TRAIN WRECKED.

Part of the Pullman train from London to the North got off the line at Heeley Station, near Sheffield, early on Wednesday morning. Banning against a signal box, and upsetting it, the carriages ploughed their way through the wooden platform, which was all but de- moliehed, and then they were overturned. A few of the passengers,—of whom there was not'a large num- ber altogether—were injured, and it is believed that the consequences would have been more serious but for the great strength of the Pullman cars. The front portion of the train, which did not leave the metals, went on to Bheffield. The fact that the express was going at the rate of fifty miles an hour when the acci- dent took place makes it all the more remarkable that the consequences were not much worse than they ap- pear to have been.

div.head: GERMAN IMPORT DUTIES ON SALT.
div.p: THE GERMAN IMPORT DUTIES ON SALT.

The owners of German salt pits, who have lately petitioned the Government for an advance of the import duties on salt, write to disclaim any associa- tion with the Pioteotionist movement as such. They assert that all they contend for is reciprocity, and par- ticularly between Germany and France. They urge thit while German salt imported into Francais charged with a duty which amounts to 80 pfennig (say 10d,) per.loo kilogrammes over the amount of the tax on French salt, tha latter is placed as regards duty in Germany in precisely the same position as the native German salt, and even enjoys an advantage over the latter equivalent to 12 pfennig in consequence of the mode of collecting the dues. They indignantly deny that they desire protection in any form; all they de- mand is that they may be placed on an equality with the foreigner.

div.head: SCALDING FATALITY IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: SCALDING FATALITY IN WARRINGTON.

Mr. Driffield held an inquest on Monday, at the General Wolfe Inn, Church-street, on the body of Jas. Foster, aged 1 year and eight months, which occurred on Saturday last, from injuries received on the pre- vious day by scalding. It appeared that the mother took a pot of boiling water off the fire, poured some of the water into a tin mug used by the child, and placed it on a table. Whilst she was in the back kitchen pouring the remaining water out of the saucepan, the child clutched the tin which had been left within its reach on the table, and precipitated its boiling contents on its breast and arms. The child was severely scalded, and died from the effects of its injuries next morning. The !Coroner reprananded the mother for her carelessness in leaving the water within the child's reach, and a verdict of "Accidental death" was re- turned by the Pry.

MURDEROUS ASSAULT • ON 'A EfAMEKEEPER AT DUNHAM. At the Altrinohara Police Court on Tuesday, befote Mr. W. loynson (chairman), Messrs. 7. Allen, B. IL Norris, and E. Joyason, Rd. Robinson Boyle, Joseph Rogerson, Chas. Bailey, Samuel Smith, By. Devonport,Bamuel Morton, By. Morton, By. Weston, Ed. Holt, Samuel Holt, James Aldoroft, alias arimes, and Thomas Holt, all of Breadheath, were charged with maliciously wounding Leonard Brown with intent to do him grievous bodily harm, at Binderland, on Sun- day, the 19th inst. The head of the prosecutor Was covered with bandages, and his face bore marks of the brutal treatment he had receiyed. He was accommo- dated with a seat whilst giving his evidence. The in- terest in the case was clearly indicated by the crowd of persons in the court. Mr. Moire, of Warrington,

appeared for all the prisoners. The prosecutor, Leonard Brown, stated that he was an under gamekeeper in the employ of Mk. Reiss, and that he lived at Binderland. Be had been in his employ since the 11th of last August. On Sunday morning, the 19th inst., he was out 'at Carrington and came ' by Broadheath with Edward Egerton ;leo & game- keeper. At Broadheath he saw Samuel Bolt oome off the fields at about twelve o'clock. He asked him what he had got in his pockets, and lie replied" No- thing for you." As he was a suspicious character, witness wanted to see what he had in Ins pooketoind they started roughly, and he searched him and found nothing in his pockets. He went away towards Broadheath village. Another man, who was with him, ran away. He (Samuel Holt) returned in about ten minutes, and there were some dozen men, amongst whom were the prisoners Grimes and Bailey. He could not recognise any more, as they ran away. They started stoning him and beating him with sticks. Samuel Holt struck him with his Mt, and Grimes flung a stone at him, which struck him on the arm. His brother, William Grimes, also struck him. Several other stones were thrown, which struck him on the legs and arms. He went for Mr. Carter, a farmer, at Dunham who came, and Edward Egerton was there. When Carter came up the men ran away. Witness ' shouted to Carter for assistance, which caused him to come up. At twenty minutes to three in the after. noon, witness Egerton, and Asnley met on Mr. Coward's lend at hinderland. ThNy separated, and were to meet at a cover called the Gorse. Witness, $ has after leaving them to go in the direction of the Gorse, when he was wining out of Mr. Howard's fielda into the highway, was fastening a gate, when Thos. Holt snatched his hat off. All the other men were waiting In the road for him. There were in the road Hoyle, s Rogerson. Smith, Samuel Morton, Henry Morton, sIPS; Weston, Ed. Holt, Samuel Holt, Aldcroft.alias Grimes, and Thomas Holt. The othe men were within a yard of witness. Thomas Holt snatched his hat off. Wit- s' , ‘s,s, ners6tried to snatch it out of Holt's hand. Witness ,a,ls asked him for his hat, and be replied "No, I'll give L you something else." Witness then raised his stick up, Xis and Thomas Holt struck him three times in the face with his fist. ' Aldorof a alias Grimes, Samuel Holt, and Ed. Bolt then struck him with sticks on the head. He identified is large stick, some two inches in diameter, and about a yard long, with which Aldoroft struck bun on the head and across the back. He struck him many times. Samuel Holt and Edward Holt were also thrashing him with sticks. These men struck him on the head and shoulders. AS they were about to leave him, Aldcrof t threw a paving stone, which struck hinipn the head and out it open. Witness felt stunned after receiviug the blows and the stone felled him to the ground. He got up and paid "You'll hear further of this my man.' Witness was walking away when Aldereft ran back to strike him, and witness received the blow on his arm. He was coming again when Welton said, stop now, "I think we have given him plenty," Aldcroft would • ,have struck him again had it not been for Weston. Ma other men who did not strike, called out "go into was going on for a quarter of an hour. They took his at ck from him, it was a white yew one. The men all went awey together in the direction of Broad- heath. Whilst this was going on he did shout out. Alter the assault witness went to James Hulmes, a !armee. The witnesses shirt, scarf, collar and jacket were produced, and ;they were saturated with blood. He had two wounds on his head from which the:bloc:4 had came. Wham felt stupilled and did not know hew be got to Holmes farm. Be came with Mr. Hulme to ;the polio* station at Altrinoham, and went to Dr. Atwell, and airs= there to the hospital. which institution he left the following morning. He still felt weak and was suffering from the wounds. Da eress-examinetion by Mr. Moore, Samuel Holt tore his Shirt and waistcoat in trying to get from wit- ness whilst he was searching him. At the meeting at noon he only recognised Samuel Holt, Aldoroft, and Bailey, AD being present on the first occasion. The big stick was not his own it was Aldcroft's. He never struck a blow with his stick nor his fist at the second meet eg. Edward and Samuel Holt were the only men who struck him in the afternoon. After receiving all the serious injuries he was able to walk to Altrin- chem. Witness was sober. He had never quarelled with these men. On the first occasion he was struck by Samuel Holt with his fist, Bailey with a etick, and Aldcroft with a stones and on the second, Samnel Holt, Edward Holt, and a ldcroft. Dr. Attwell, of Altrincham, stated that prosecutor was brought to him with his face, head, and clothes, covered with blood. Ile had received two severe ecalp wounds, two on the right temple, and a severe bruise on the back of the head. The scalp wounds were bleeding. There were bruises and marks on the back and shoulders. He dressed the wounds, and as they had bled freely and were Wrely. to bleed again he sent him to the hospital. The bruises and wounds would result from blows from sticks. Edward Egerton gamekeeper for Mr. Reiss, deposed to finding three dam, produced. William Ashley, gamekeeper to Mr. Reiss, identified eiekt of the prisoners. P.C. Hoyle stated that Devonport said that he was there, but didn't do anything. The keeper had to use his stick terribly to keep the men off him. Inspector Leighton charged the prisoners. when Boyle said he was about 300 yards away, and he never did anything, but in the forenoon the keeper threw him down on his back. Rogerson said "I was with Boyle at the time. I never touched him." Bailey said that In the afternoon he knew nothing about it, and he was not out, but in the forenoon be was with Boyle. The keeper beat Samuel Holt, I went up and he struck me with his stick, and threw me dawn. Smith said "I know nothing about it." Davenport said" I was having a walk and saw what took place, he never touched me, and I never touched him.' Samuel Morton said" Me and Devonport were having a walk out when the keeper and Thomas Holt were having words about a hat, the keeper struck at Thomas Holt, and Edward here guarded the blow off his brother, or he would have struck him on the head with a stick. This was in the afternoon. By. Morton said : I was not far off at the time. I saw By. Weston go to stop Grimes (Aldcroft) from hitting him witlashis stick. By. Weston said: I saw Grimes hitting the keeper with his stick. I told him :to leave off, he had done enough. Ed. Holt said: I was there, and looked on, and in- spected, and saw it. He struck at my brother, and I . broke his blow off. Samuel Holt said : We were all together in the fore- noon. The keeper struck me with his stick, and tore my shirt off and waistcoat. In the afternoon I was there ; no one ever touched the keeper only Grimes. He apprehended Aldcroft or Grimes on the previous day,"`and charged him, he said, "I was not the man who touched the keeper first, so let it be fair play. I do know the man who struck the keeper first. I was a hundred yards away. There Would have been no bother at all only for Sam Bolt; he shouted us to as- sist him in the forenoon, and caused us :to meet in the afternoon." Thomas Holt was charged that morning. He said the keeper was on the high road. He had my hat, and my brother Edward asked him for it. lie said he would not give it to him. Mr. Moore, for the prisoners, submitted that there stem not a tittle of evidertoe against Hoyle, Rogerson, Smith, Bailey. By. Devonport, Samuel Morton, Henry Weston, and Thomas Holt, of unlawful wounding. As the bench would probably commit some of the pri- soners he would not go into their defence. The bench retired to consider their verdict, and on returning into court the Chairman stated that the bench had decided to commit for trial at th 3 sessions Thomas Bolt, Samuel Holt, Ed. Holt, and Aldcroft Miss Grimes. Tbe other prisoners would be dis- charged. Au application for their release on bail was do. °lined.

A meeting under the auspices of the church of Eng. land Temperance Society, was held in the Literary Institution, Altzincham, on Monday evening. On Sunday reference was made to the cense of Temper- ance in many of the churches in the neighbourhood.

The Rev. CANON, BAIXECALY speaking at Bowdon Church on Sunday morning, took for his text Ephesians v., 18. "And be not drunk with •- wine, wherein is °mien ; but be filled withthe Spirit." However much they might deem that the cireumstances of the Church of Ephesus rendered expressly necessary the warning of the text, still in every age the profound wisdom of it would be apparent. However much they might differ from each other In natural temperament, so that One man might be saved from the sin of covetous- nees, while he readily gave way to drunkenness or lust, still there was an evil principle in them all—an evil principle inherited from our first patents, which, tin- .lese prayer, and watchfulness, and God's Holy Spirit Prevented, would land them in the most debasing temptations. The world, the flesh, and the devil, that tried so sorely the first Christians, were Piet as dan- gerous now. The exhortation of St. Paul in the text was as needful now as when he made it, now that this 'temptation to drunkenness the besetting sin of England—was still a constant cause of every kind of Crime. There was hardly any other sin which seized all sorts and conditions of men, alike the rich and the poor, the gross and the refined, the talented and the ignorant, the recluse and the Man of the world, to fall under its mysterious and fatal spell. It threw its coils around the man of brilliant intellect, and bound him in the same bondage as it did the fin- unlettered savage. It enthralled the rich and the. noble, and it became the means of purchasing thsir own uthrery and everlasting death. Its false light fell on the youth of promise, and his fair prospects were -blighted, and the hopes of his family were dashed down in bitter disephointment. It laid hold of the man et vigorous usefulness, and his powers were crippled from doing good, and he did harm to his neighbours. And since that sin was so universel, who should say that he might not himself fall a victim to if? Did any so pride themselves on their strict and moderated habits in the past, or on their spiritual attainments, to say, "Is thy servant a dog that he shall do this thing ?" He would only say that people who deemed themselves as safe as they deemed them- selves to be had, nevertheless, slipped down step by step; and therefore it could not be out of place to re- iterate the Apostle's warning, even to an assembly of professing Christians many of whom were "old stagers" as they might say, and had made great ad- vances in tee Christian life," Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess, .fee.'•' And it was thought to be ne- cessary in every rant of life and every stage of Chris- tian attainment, that for them own sakes, and as a matter of precaution, and far the sake of others by why of example ani precept, he would exheet them to join the Church of England Temperande Society, whose cause he was privileged to advocate that day. The Rev. Cerium Gone who preached in the afternoon from the text: I, Cc rinthians, ix. chap. 25th verve, "Every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things," said the sin brought before them that day was, he would not Bay the sin of drunkenness, for he hoped he might say that most of those who came to the House of God were not so far tempted as to be drunkards; but the sin of the intemperate use of God's gift of wine. He wished to speak with all liberality and with all truth on that matter, and he had said God's gift of wine, for wine was God's gift. Corn, and wine, and oil were the three blessings which were so promised in God's word to God's people. And if, in a day like our own, a day after all et abounding wealth among all classes, amongst Workingmen and women if they knew it, as well as and sometimes more than amongst others, there was a danger lest the very bounties of God, the very freeness with which His 'gifts were given, lest that very freeness should lead no into the very ungrateful abuse of them. He asked everyone —and there was ' this advantage that the answer might be given silently in their own hearts ; but let it be spoken truthfully— was there the slighted temptation to anyone there to- wards the excessive use, that was the abuse of wine? He thought the most mishief was done by secret, un- seen drinking. He tdid not think that the mischief was anything like so great—he had almost. said that in our day no mischief at all—was done wheu wine was used in men's company, and when wine was used alto- gether for hospitable and social purposes. He was persuaded that this gift of God of wine was intended at ouch times to be present on our tables. He knew, and they knew, that he should not be following his Master, or not representing him aright, if he denied tins fact. But all the while let him say, that as wine had its place in their marriage feasts and other feasts of joy, so Christ had His place also, and he ought to be present in their homes, and He ought to be binding them at all such times in holy companionship of love. Wine was ennobled te,be the symbol of His best gifts. Should he, then, take that which was the sign and the pledge of the blood of the Son of God, and debauch and slay hie soul therewith ? What words through all eternity could express the sinfulness of that deed ? One might think that by totally abstaining from the use of that which had doubtless been grievously abused he could best give the hand of fellowship to a weak and fallen brother; another man might think by temperately continuing to use this gift he would set a higher example still. Let every man be fully per- suaded in his own mind before God, and then let him act; but let no one act for one moment with a view to self-indulgence. Let them, every man, con- . eider the welter° of another, and then God's blessing would come back to their own souls if they acted under His guidance, in fulaesp and sich.4ese and abid- ing grace,

THE CHESHIRE FARMER AND THE MA.RKET INSPECTOR. An amusing incident transpired in the Warrington market yesterday, which resulted in a Cheshire farmer being outwitted through his own folly, and which prevented the perpetration of a gross fraud upon the Warrington publics. It appears that one at these cul- tivators of our Cheshire acres had the &luck to lose a cow by death, and anxious to avoid pecuniary loss, he made his way to Warrington market, where he ex- pected to dispose of it to some " enterprising" butcher. When in the market he came across Mr. Place, the market inspector, to whom he confidingly told his story, and asked him if he could recommend him a butcher who would buy the dead cow "on the quiet," ad if he could, he wouldn't mind standing him a "good thing." As Mr. Place's principles do not tend to the absorption of " drinks " of any intoxicat- ing quality. the offered bribe was useless; but in spite of that diawback, be good naturedly told the farmer that he could introduce him to a man who did a regular trade in deceased and diseased meat, and who would be sure to buy the carcase." The farmer was delighted at his good fortune. and Mr. Place at once introduced him to his friend Mr. Norman, the sanitary inspector. A bargain was at once made, and although the case was beyond the Warrington inspector's juris- diction, Mr. Bawling, the rural sanitary inspector, was informed of the circumstances, who adopted such steps as to prevent any further negotiation on the part of the farmer. On discovering that the biter had been bitten, his rage and disappointment were excessive. He has since judiciously resolved to confide his pro- ponds in regard to the "dead meat market" exclu- sively to persons who have more sympathy with such transactions, and to be more cautious in future as to the time and "Place" where they shall be negotiated. At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, another .of these serious stabbing cases, which are exceedingly prolific amongst the Irish portion of the population, came before the Bench. It appeared from the evidence that the prisoner, Gerald Newman, went home from his work the worse for drink, and when having his tea he commenced to quarrel with a fellow-lodger. The prosecutor, Michael Carroll, interposed, and en- deavoured to pacify the prisoner, when seizing a knife Irons the table he stabbed Carroll in two places on the right arm, indicting very serious injuries. Dr. King who dreseed the wounds said the prosecutor was still in a dangerous condition, and he was afraid that erysipelas might set in. div.p: DISGUSTING ELOPEDIENT AT WAR. BINGTON.

Au elopement of a particularly infamous character has taken place at Warrington, where the wife of a beerhouse keeper has distinguished herself by running sway with her nephew! It appears the unhappy hus- band ie about 60 yeers of age, and his wife some 20 years his junior. Although in very comfortable cir. cumstancee the course of their married life has not run smoothly, owing to his wife'. vagaries, she having lip. parently' a penchant for running away, a feat she has accomplished three times, and each occasion has found her a fresh compagnon de voyage. Each time her has- band forgave her, although her conduct was such as to incur the reprobation of her neighbours, who publicly burnt her in effigy. A short time ago the old man's nephew, 22 years of age, took up his abode with the family, and pretended to pay his addresses to his con • sin, a girl of 16. The father thought the mother encouraged the suit, who with the young couple often took drives into the country, but invariably at pater. families expense. However, the wife and her nephew conducted their amours so glaringly .as to attract the attention of the husband, who ordered his nephew out of the house. During the husband's temporary absence the wife and he procured a, cab, and stripping the house of everything of value left the husband to his fate, the six children also accompanying their mother. Upon their flight being discovered, a'. enraged was the husband that he sold his bone for £760, which is said to be £260 below its value, disposed of hie business and "cried her notchel," resolved that this disgrace to the name of woman should pollute his hearth no mom The wretched creature is said to be now living with tier rascally paramour somewhere in Widnes. div.head: EASTERN QUESTION.
div.p: THE EASTERN QUESTION.

IT seems very difficult if not impossible to avoid thinking very anxiously about the state of affairs in Turkey. Painful recollec- tions of the Crimean war will keep constantly recurring to the mind, and tiage and in- fluence the intere,4 with which we view the present complications lin the East. To say that the I astern questien is among the foremost topics of d seussion is to say little. It is a mere fact that it takes up, for the time, the w .ole ground of politics. The state of matters at present appears to be this. The Russo-Servian army having fought for the defence of their country, have been outnumbered and pressed up from one line of defence to another, until the whole of t e State seemed to be in a fair way for being over run and desolated by the Turkish army. As no European Power wished tD see the Turks in possession of Servia, the 1 Porte consented, after remonstrances of a more or icts friendly character, to abstain from pushing their advantage any further, to suspend hostilities and agree to an armis- tice. The armistice however, could con- clude nothing of itself, but during the time that it was to last, a conference was to be held of diplomatic representatives of all the great European Powers, and of the Turkish Government, to enquire not only into the causes of the war, but into the grievances of the Christian inhabitants of the Northern parts of Turkel. Considerable difficulty has been found in inducing the Porte to submit to this, but it has been arranged, somehow, he Conference is to be held, and the Marquis of Salisbury has gone to attend it, and re- present this country at Constantinople. Now, for all that we have said, there would not appear to be much room for any doubt or scruple at all about the matter. But the question lies much deeper. This country, for reasons now long forgotten or obsolete has for many years past been the ally and friend of Turkey, screened her faults, fought for her against seeming oppression, and, strongest test of all, lent her money. Although we knew that the Turks professed Mahometanisra, and not only pro- fessed it but acted up to its principles, one of which is that no Christian whatever can have his word or oath taken against that of a Mus- sulman, or be other than a slave or object of contempt to him, and that another is that their religion must be propagated by fire and sword,— although we knew all this, yet this our England, which would in some res- pects seem to have arrogated to itself an exclusive ownership of Christianity, chose to foster and succour the Turkish Government, and protect it from all corners, and let it seethe on in its inconceivable wickedness.

Servia, once a province of Turkey, but for some time past freed from all but a nominal dependence upon Turkish power, began the struggle. Herzegovina has broken her bonds asunder, and victoriously resisted every effort again to enchain her. Of Bul- garia, we know of an abortive rising, rather than an insurrection, whLh has been quelled in a manner which, showing the Turk in his true colours has sickened us of our ally, and converted him into an object of disgust and hatred. At least, one would have thought so, but our Tory Government, faith- ful to its traditions, although neglectful of the country's voice, continues to pat him on the back, and clamour for the integrity and independence of Turkey. Any opposition to this they call party feeling, and indeed, have so scared some honest Liberals with the taunt as to induce them to disclaim any ap- proach to party feeling in the matter. Mr. Leathern, however, speaking at Huddersfield on Tuesday night, very fairly disposed of this view. " What is party ?" he asks. "Is party a mere cabal for selfish or sordid ends, or is it not the result of the highest ambition which can actuate any men who hold opinions which they believe to be for the national welfare, and for the promotion of that cause of justice which is the cause of all throughout the world ?" And he went on to show that there were two sides to this question, and that the side which had been adopted by the Government was not the side which had been adopted by the people at large. "It is necessary to maintain the integrity and independence of Turkey," say the '1 ories. But the Liberals say, "It is necessary to secure the lives and liberties of the Christians, whatever may happen to the integrity and independence of Turkey." Here, then, we are brought up straight to the Eastern question. It is no longer asked, "Is Turkey to be allowed to go on doing as she has done ?" but, assuming that she is not to be so allowed, how are the lives and liberties of the Christians to be secured in those provinces still belonging to Turkey? The Conference that is to meet is to settle this, if it can. Our special Ambassador is ng counsel by the way, on his journey to Constan:'aople. He has had an interview in Paris with eFrench Minister for Foreign Affairs, of which could not but know beforehand the result. ... Frenchman, of -.:re for ,any- whatever politics, has any atip thing outside France but her lost proviZea of Alsace and Lorraine. On Wednesday he called at Berlin, where Bismarck came specially to meet him, and which the Em- peror William and family left at the same time, speoially not to meet him. Prince Bis- marck is not in the habit of telling anybody very much of what he thinks, and so, being left to guess, we may imagine that he had rather the thing hadn't happened, but that if Russia and Turkey should go ta war he will be able to side with the winner, and get something from the loser, and look forward to coming by his own as an honest man ex- pects to do when certain things happen. Nothing can be expected to come of a visit to Vienna where Lord Salisbury is at the present moment. The Austro-Hungarian t Empire is a kingdom divided against itself. The Kaiser is, to use a homely comparison, in the position &_f a householder who has a bailiff in the house and a fire next door. But before the Conference can meet, the question may be in process of settlement in another way. Ihe Emperor Alexander may, like his namesake, have cut this Gordian knot with the sword. The Russian Emperor has expressed his intentions very plainly in- deed. He is dissatisfied with the dilatori- ness of the Turkish Government, and is de- termined to be put off no longer. Unless Europe is prepared to act with firmness and energy, he will be obliged, he says, to act , alone, and since then he has placed a large I part of his army upon a war footing, and ' appointed his brother, the Grand Duke Con- stantine, to assume the command on the very day named for the asserubli g of the Con- ference. With a Russian army drawn up on its northern boundaries, and a British fleet lying under the very windows of its capital, there is one thing that Turkey need not fear —she is tolerably free from molestation by anybody else. Although the Judges at Westminster are said to I be overdone with work, and have a long list of causes in arrear, they do not seem willing to part with any trifle that comes before them as long as there is anything to be got out of it, as the follow- ing will perhaps show :—A meeting of shareholders in a mining company had been duly called, and one shareholder only attended. He took the chair, made a call of 4s. 6d. a share, passed a resolution that all cheques on the company's bankers should be signed by himself, and to wind up, carried a vote of thanks to himself for his able and courteous conduct, in the chair. An action having been brought against a shareholder for payment of the call thus made, two of the Judges decided that the call was made at a regular meeting, and must be paid. The shareholder appealed against this, and four other Judges held that there must be at least two to meet each other and so form a meeting, for one share- holder could not meet himself, and there was special or technical meaning in the word "meeting." " No," said the Lord Justice Mellish, "we must go by the ordinary signification of language." Good, my Lord Justice, only persuade your legal brethren to go on in that style, and we shall hear no more of arrears. Up to now, common sense would seem to be in arrear as well as the cause list.

A few years since we published a journal or series of letters describing "A journey on horseback from Warrington to the Lakes," by an ancestor of the Crosfields, of Warrington. The "Journey on horse- back" was made a century since. About the same time an English judge was penning another journal not devoid of interest. "Judge Curwen's Journal, describing his experiences in Lancashire and Che- shire in 1777 and 1780" is being republished under the head of "Local Gleaninge," by a Manchester contemporary. From the " Journal "we gather that in June, 1777, Judge Curwen visited Munches. ter, Chester, and Warrington. The few words about Warrington, "the gutter running through the middle" of the streets and the abundance of " dis- senters," who have an academy for young preachers of that persuasion," is suggestive. Thanks to the Warrington Corporation the open gutters have gone, and although the " Academy " is no more, the dis- senters (of whom at that very time Mr. Crosfield, the Lake journalist, was one), continue to flourish and abound even more than they did a hundred yearB since. Judge Curwen says—" Having taken a view of the whole place, we took leave of Chester, design- ing for Manchester by way of Duke of Bridgewater's canal from Warrington; on that route our first stage was Frodsham, an indifferent small village, distance en miles. The keeper of the inn, an Irishman, not wanting in the characteristic mark of that country, a bold, unblushing face; after a plausible commen- dation of his carriages and horses he gave us a sorry post-chaise and a pair of miserable cattle ; he yet had the impudence to apply to us to procure the road from Warrington to this paltry village to be made a turnpike, saying it would be pounds in his pocket, which I really doubt. He mistook us for parliament men. From hence to Warrington ten miles; the Inn, the Red Lion,' tolerable. Streets narrow, and ill paved; like many other towns, with a gutter running through the middle, rendering it inconvenient passing the streets. This town abounds in dissenters, and has an academy for young preachers of that persuasion."

The last survivor of the " Victory " one Of the Trafalgar ships was noted last week. I observe that another "last survivor" has turned Up in the inter- val. But there is always another survivor of a famous battle until survivorship is chronologically impossible. I prefer to stick to old Chapman who has just died at Dundee. Poor fellow ! One's feeling towards a hero who has never been hurt, and who dies quietly in his bed at the absurd ago of ninety two, is of a somewhat mixed character. He may not exactly be an impostor but one somehow feels that we should almost like him better if he had reposed on his laurels earlier. "Whom the gods love die young." It doesn't ap- pear as if Chapman had achieved so much as a broken shin! The fellow never bled for his coun- try! To be sure, people from Dundee are not ad- dicted to "bleeding." One wonders, however, that poor Chapman didn't contrive to get a pension —a kind of thing perhaps to whish Dundee folk are addicted. A very small wound would have entitled this Trafalgar hero to a quarterly allowance. Some theatrical lover exclaims "My wound is great be- cause it is SO small." "Yet," retorted one of the audi- ence, who resented the lady's affectation, "Yet 'twould be greater were it none at all." In view of the missing pension, poor Chapman could have em- ployed the latter line with much propriety. Seeing that our Dundee veteran was discharged from the navy 62 years since, a pension of a shilling a day would have made a pretty sum by this time, and Walkinghame only knows what the compound interest would have come to ? It might have made a little hole in Mr. Disraeli's favorite "flea-bite " the National Debt. An address upon international arbitration was de- livered at Llandudno, on Wednesday evening, by the Rev. W. Glover, of Manchester. At the close of the lecture Mr. Bright, who is now staying at Llandudno, fpoke in support of the principles advocated by Mr. Glover. The right honourable gentleman re- ferred to the disastrous effects which had been pro- duced upon this country by war, and said that seeing what was paid for the Crimean war, and seeing how great a crime we then committed, it was as- tounding that there should be any man, much more that the Prime Minister of the country, should, by his unadvised and unwise speaking, Invite the nation to involve itself in another war which might be as prolonged and as costly as the last, and would undoubtedly be as great a failure. There was nothing in our position, three thousand miles from Constantinople, to justify a ,fear of Russia. He re- joiced to believe that Were was still hope of peace, and he thought that the conversation between the English Minister and the Emperor of Russia, reported in that day's papers, put it beyond a doubt that the Czar was as anxious for peace as any statesman of either party In this country.

Mr. Cross, Home Secretary, visited Birmingham on Monday, and was present in the evening at a banquet in the Town Hall. Responding to the toast of " Her Majesty's Ministers," the right honourable gentleman said no Mtnister who was in his BESLIPI3I3 could dePire anything but peace. The Government from the first had had but that one desire. They tried to prevent the war, and when it broke out they tried to keep it localised. Other counsels which had been brought for- ward were fraught with the deepest danger to this country, and to the whole of Europe. When the Con- ference met there would be an end—for the present at any rate, and he hoped for all time—of the dangerous practice of treaty breaking. Treaties might be modi- fied on bases agreed upon by all parties. All the Cabinets of Europe had thought that, by going into the Conference, they had the means of settling the question, and he (Mr. Cross) was quite willing to leave tile various opinions which had been promulgated to take care of themselves.

Mr. Cross brought his sojourn in Birmingham to a close on Wednesday. In the morning he paid a visit to the area which has been scheduled by the Corpora- tion under the Artisans' Dwellings Act. Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., in proposing his health, spoke in eulogistic terms of the views upon social and sanitary improvements expressed by Mr. Cross in his speech to the working men. Mr. Cross, in responding, avoided all allusion to political questions, and reiterated his opinion in favour of throwing additional responsibilities upon the muni- cipalitiea themselves.

div.head: lIIGH JINKS AT THE ASHTON RINK.
div.p: lIIGH JINKS AT THE ASHTON RINK.
From the 31-anehecter Critic of To-day.

All lovers of their country will be glad to hear that in the happy hamlet of Ashton-on-Mersey. we are progressing. Within the last few years we have put up and pail for a good looking and spacious church (we had previously a good-locking and apaciou3 rec- tor), and on Tuesday evening lest Mr. joynson inau- gurated a new ekating rink, so that aftcr airing our souls at the new church, we can now extend our bodies ' at the new rink, that is to say, those can who please. The writer of these presents, however, must decline, , for physical reasons, to it along an asphalte floor on rollers, unless supported arm in arm by two directors of the institution, with a casual churchwarden as a rear guard. It will thus be seen that in commending this rink at Ashton, as we now do, to all and sundry, we are not actuated by selfish considerations. But if we don't avail ourselves of its advantages, the youngsters at home may; and we can safely say that if our scna, during their minority, or even afterwards, should not select any physical recreation inferior to a E katis g ' rink, we shall have no cause of complaint, nor can we very well understand the objections which are enter- tamed in some quarters to this kind of amusement. So far from considering it any disadvantage that young men and young women should enjoy this pas- time in common, we should deem it rather a gain of great moment—especially to the young men—that they should have in a larger measure than heretofore during their leisure hours the refining and modu- lating influences of their feminine friends and acquain- tances. From what we have seen of the conduct of the Ai- ton rink, there is no danger of its -becoming a sort of liberty hall. Of course we all know that parents and guardians are the best monitors of youth—as well when it is at play as when it is at work; and in saying this we would counsel the parents and guardians whose youngsters frequent this place to do that which the directors cannot do, because they have no authority, siz. ; to exercise a fair but not too strict an amount of control over this amusement, by dropping in occa- sionally themselves and supervising the situation now and then.

So on Tuesday we had high jinks at the formal opening of the rink some twelve hundred people being present. The civil, the military, and the eccle- siastical authorities put in an appearance.; the rank such as it is, and the fashion such as it is, of Sale and Ashton, fertilised the auspicious occasion. The terri- torial aristocracy mingled loosely with the ordinary parishioner, ana he did not attempt to quilt him. At the sound of a band-bell, which seemed to require a cry of muffins as its proper complement, there was a partial lull in the weaving-shed noise which the rinkers make with their skates. Then Mr. Nicholas Silvert, the chairman of the limited company, to whose public spirit we are indebted for the rink, made a short speech, introducing Mr. Joyneon, who made a long one. After this the Rector favoured us with a few canine experiences from Birmingham, whereat there was a good deal of ruuken applause. We had ex- pected epeches from Mr. .1. H. Lynde and Mr. Edward Bellhouse, respectively the architect and engineer of the building, but the civil and ecclesiastical authorities were too many for them. We endeavoured ourselves to remedy this mischief by proposing the health or Mr. Lynde and Mr. Bellhouse privately, in a neat glass of Most at the charge or the company, in an unosten- tatious cabin under the gallery, and we are pleased to state that in that restricted apartment all went merry as a marriage bell. Mr. Ingram, of Beaufort Grange, the well-known magistrate, and ourselves, formed a select circle round a bottle of Moat, and in this happy union of glasses, the high and the low, the rich and the poor, we remark symptoms of the approach of a milennium.

The situation of the AShton rink is excellent. It stands almost in the mid t of a nursery garden, where youthful shrubs are being brought up for useful occupations in after life. In this it has a great ad- vantage over the New Church, which is at present flanked with a large field of cabbages in an advanced stage of decomposition, thus communicating to the service of our beloved Church the temporary flavour of pickles. But St. Mary agdalene has the pull of the rink in the possession of a splendid bell; so that the people of Oakfield are pining for priveleges which are vouchsafed to those in Moss-Jane cornucopiously. Therefore, let us wish for success to the Ashton skating rink, and may those who use it glide as eabily and smoothly over the inequalities of the pathway of their respective lives, as the. y do over the skating floor in Ashton-lane, always remembering that as in sinking so in human life we must all do our utmost not to come a cropper at the end.

div.head: MALE IMPERSONATOR AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: A MALE IMPERSONATOR AT WARRINGTON.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, a brawny, masculine looking woman, named Harriet Davies, who was dressed in male attire, was charged with drunkenness and disorderly conduct. It was stated by Inspeotor Singleton that the prisoner, who habitually wears the dress characteristic of the male sex, was seen in the streets with her hands in her pockets, smoking a short pipe, and was surrounded by a mob of some hundreds of persons, who were aware of her real sox. It transpired that the worian's hus- band was an American captain, and after his death she assumed the sailor's garb, and served under Cap- tain Semmes on board the Alabama during the cele- brated Southern blockade. After running daring risks at sea, she abandoned the service of Neptune for the more peaceful and less dangerous service of Ceres, and for some years she has worked for various farmers in Cheshire and Lancashire as a man servant, her skill at the plough and her Amazonian strength in agricultu- ral work assisting her to maintain her assumed charac- ter without suspicion. THE ATHANASIAN CREED CONDEMNED.

The weekly meeting of the S. James's Mutual Im- provement Society was held in the Schoolroom on Monday evening, Mr. S. Chandley presiding, when a paper was read by the Rev. Edward H. Thomas, 8.A., on" The Use of the Athanasian Creed." After a spirited discussion, he moved the following resolution, "That it is desirable to discontinue the use of the Athanasian Creed in the public worship of the Church of England." An amendment was proposed as fol- lows—" That this society desires to record its opinion that the Athanasian Creed is founded upon most cer- tain warrant of Holy Scripture, and ought thoroughly to be received and believed, and deprecates any at- tempt to put an end to its recital in the public services of the Church of England." The amendment, on being put to the meeting, found very few supporters, so that the original resolution was carried by a large majority amidst loud applause.
NOVEL REQUEST OF A DEBATING SOCIETY.

The subject for discussion at the meeting of this Society, held on Monday evening, at the Schoolroom, Latchford, Warrington, was "Light Literature and its Influence," introduced by Mr. Chas. Peake. The essayist argued that the light literature, by which term he meant the penny miscellanies which are circulated so freely through the country of the present day, has an injurious effect upon the minds of those who read it, and concluded by moving the following resolution: " That this society is of opinion that th,3 light litera- ture now in circulation is calculated to injure the minds of the youth of this Country; " which, after an animated discussion, was carried. The debate next Monday will be opened by the Rev. E. H. Thomas, on " The Athanasian Creed." Daring the discussion several speakers spoke in terms of condemnation of newspaper proprietors resorting to the practice of vitf. ating the minds of their readers by inserting navels of a sensational character into their columns. This, it was said, tended to encourage the taste for novel read- ing, and was productive of much mischief. At the conclusion of the debatl a resolution was adopted re- questing the editor of the Warrington Guardian to dis- continue the sensational novel now in course of publication in its columns on the grounds named. A paragraph reporting the proceedings, including a copy of the resolution, was forwarded to the editor of the paper in question, who will, doubtless, forthwith com- municate with Miss Braddon and arrange for the withdrawal of the offending fiction,

div.head: DEATH OF A FORMER WARRINGTON MINISTER.
div.p: DEATH OF A FORMER WARRINGTON MINISTER.

The announcement of the death of the Rev. John Morris, who was formerly a superintendent of the Warrington Wesleyan circuit, will be received by the members of that denomination with much regret. The deceased gentleman spent three years in Warrington, which is the utmost limit allowed by the Wesleyan con- ference, and was highly respected by his people. About a year ago through ill-health he retired from the regu. lar work of the ministry, and took up his residenCe in the neighbourhood of Bradford, where he died on the 15th inst., in the 65th year of his age, and in the 42nd year of his ministry. The late Mr. Morris was one of the few remaining links which conneet the Methodism of to-day with the za,il and fervour which distinguished the ministrations of its preachers half a century ago. As a sound doctrinal preacher Mr. Morris had but few equals, his sermons always giving evidence of careful thought and studious reseal...fa. His eloquence in the pulpit was remarkably effective, and during his labours in Warrington there was a marked increase in church membership. The rev, gentleman was never ashamed of his origin, but rather prided himself in the fact that from a poor Lancashire cotton spinner he had, through Uod's pro.. vidence and his own energy, achieved a position of honour and credit in the Wesleyan ministry. As an instance of his thirst for religious knowledge, he would relate how in his youth he walked a dozen miles after finishing his day's work, for the purpose of bor- rowing a volume or. Wesley's Sermons. In the Che- shire portion of the circuit Mr. Morris was also highly esteemed, and his death will be a source of regret to the Wesleyaus of Warrington and. the neighbourhood generally.
